claims.text: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy has high strength through solid-solution strengthening.
The untreated alloy has a relatively homogeneous microstructure.
The untreated alloy has limited ductility and non-uniform plastic deformation.
Adding 1–3 at.% of a ductility-enhancing element and applying a tailored heat treatment will generate fine, coherent nanoscale precipitates.
Optimized heat treatment can favor homogeneous precipitate nucleation and prevent precipitate coarsening.
The intervention will produce uniformly distributed precipitates both at grain boundaries and within grains.
The nanoscale precipitates will impede crack propagation.
The nanoscale precipitates will facilitate dislocation mobility.
The precipitates will reduce local stress concentrations.
Reduced stress concentrations and facilitated dislocation motion will enable more uniform plastic deformation.
The precipitates will continue to reinforce the high-strength refractory matrix.
The treated alloy will have greater elongation than the untreated baseline.
The treated alloy will have a more uniform strain distribution than the untreated baseline.
The treated alloy's yield strength will remain within approximately ±5–10% of the untreated baseline.
The treated alloy's impact-induced energy release will remain within approximately ±5–10% of the untreated baseline.
The proposed benefits should occur at ambient or moderately elevated temperatures where plastic deformation occurs.
Over-doping, precipitate coarsening, or intergranular embrittlement may negate the proposed benefits.
Precedent studies in similar systems support the qualitative effects of precipitate engineering.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis targets preservation of impact-induced energy release, but the falsification rule switches to impact energy absorption. Release and absorption are not interchangeable response variables, so the decisive impact criterion is internally inconsistent.

The hypothesis is explicitly conditional on successfully producing fine, coherent precipitates, yet the rule treats precipitate coarsening or inhomogeneity as falsification. Those observations can instead show that the specified intervention was not successfully realized, rather than falsifying its conditional causal claim.
